---
title: "Rank and the Invertible Matrix Theorem"
description: "A compact linear-algebra lesson with mathematical definitions, real values and reasoning."
---

## Start with a question

If a machine maps a whole flat sheet onto one line, can we recover which point on the sheet was the original?

## Understand the central idea

Invertibility means no information is lost. Rank tells us how many independent output directions remain.

## Express it with mathematics

$$
\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \ker(A)=\{\mathbf0\}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** rank(A) is the number of independent columns (equivalently, the dimension of the image); n is the number of input dimensions for an n×n matrix; ker(A) is the set of inputs mapped to zero; 0 is the zero vector; the double arrow means the two statements are equivalent in the square case.

**Substitute real numbers:** A=[[1,2],[2,4]] sends input (−2,1) to (0,0): first output −2+2=0, second −4+4=0. This nonzero input belongs to the kernel; rank is only 1, so the matrix is not invertible.

## Why this works

If a nonzero vector maps to zero, adding it to any input does not change the output. Multiple different inputs therefore have the same image. For a square n×n matrix, full rank, trivial kernel and invertibility are equivalent.

## What can go wrong?

The rank condition for rectangular matrices needs care. A 3×2 matrix can have full column rank 2 without having a two-sided square inverse.

## Your turn

Find a nonzero vector in the kernel of [[3,6],[1,2]].
